title: US hit by wave of outages: Microsoft, flights, banks and NSA hit – are they connected?
summary: Microsoft, FAA, and Chase outages highlight vulnerabilities in critical systems From disrupted emails and grounded flights to delayed bank transactions, a series of technical failures has affected major US services over five days. The disruptions have hit technology companies, airlines, financial institutions and government systems, raising questions about the reliability of critical digital infrastructure. The latest incident involves NSA Net, a highly classified communications network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA). Six people familiar with the matter told CNN that the network had gone down. There is currently no evidence that the NSA outage was caused by a cyberattack. The agency has introduced staggered arrival times for personnel while assessing the extent of the problem. Here is a breakdown of the major outages, when they happened and what caused them. November 12: Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other services. November 13: A nationwide FAA ground stop halted US flight departures for about four hours. November 13: Workday experienced a service disruption affecting access to HR and payroll tools. November 16: JPMorgan Chase customers reported transaction delays, with some payments involving other banks also affected. November 16: United Airlines experienced a systemwide outage that briefly delayed departures. November 17: CNN reported that the NSA's classified internal communications network, NSA Net, was down. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage disrupted several services, leaving users struggling to access emails and workplace tools. The disruption began on November 12 and lasted nearly 24 hours, with services restored on Friday morning, according to Microsoft's preliminary incident report. Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna attributed the outage to a combination of: Microsoft has more than 430 million Microsoft 365 users worldwide. This figure represents its user base, not the number of people affected by the outage. A technical failure affecting the US air traffic control system led the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to order a nationwide ground stop for departing flights. The rare order halted take-offs for about four hours. It was lifted at 8.15pm Eastern time on Friday (1.15am GMT on Saturday). According to AFP, it was only the second nationwide halt to take-offs since the September 11 attacks. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said an ageing system had become overloaded. title: Outages at banks, airlines, Microsoft raise security concerns
summary: During the past five days, major system crashes have disrupted email, air travel, and banking services in Massachusetts and across the country, raising concerns about digital security and how prepared companies and individuals are for such events. The disruptions began Thursday when Microsoft Outlook crashed , shutting down email access for millions of businesses. On Friday, an air traffic control crisis caused travel disruptions that lasted through the weekend . By Monday, several of the nation’s largest banks reported major outages . All systems are now back online, but experts say it is difficult to determine exactly what is happening. Consumers, however, are particularly alarmed when disruptions involve their money. "Anything that touches money is the most concerning," one expert said. "Not to be conspiratorial, but when too many things happen at the same time, it’s difficult not to be." In the latest outage, Chase Bank reported that a software bug in its hardware system caused the disruption, which affected online banking. As of Monday night, transactions were processing normally again, and the bank confirmed the outage was not the result of a cyberattack. MIT Information and Technologies Professor Stuart Madnick said the recent outages highlight how unprepared companies and individuals can be when critical services fail. "We as individuals need to realize these things can happen, whether it’s by accident or on purpose, and put in place preparations for what we would do if something happens," Madnick said. Experts recommend using multi-factor authentication, avoiding the reuse of passwords, and keeping some emergency cash on hand to protect against potential disruptions. The Chase outage primarily affected its customers, as well as customers at other banks attempting transactions with Chase. However, the issue has been resolved.

title: Why are web systems going down nationwide? Trump administration warns of more outages
summary: The FBI and Google warn that artificial intelligence is accelerating cyberattacks. The FBI and Google warn that artificial intelligence is accelerating cyberattacks. The Trump administration is suggesting new technology may be overwhelming aging computer systems as a string of outages disrupts everything from banking and air travel to national security networks. But cybersecurity experts say that may not explain all the disruptions. Meanwhile, new warnings from the FBI and Google reveal how artificial intelligence is making cyberattacks faster and more sophisticated. "I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "They're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system a little bit, and it's not able to catch up. But it has nothing to do with cyberattacks," he added. Gregory Falco, a Cornell University assistant professor of aerospace and systems engineering, said Mullin's explanation is possible but questioned whether it accounts for all the recent outages. "That doesn't happen for all of these systems overnight. So I think it has to be something a little deeper than that," Falco said. Falco cautioned that he could only speculate about the cause of the disruptions but raised the possibility of Iranian cyberattacks. "Iran has gotten really good at getting in some deep network somewhere. I think we shouldn't discount that," Falco said. Falco also suggested software updates involving AI could be causing cascading failures. There is no confirmed evidence linking Iran or other malicious actors to the recent outages. Congressional Democrats are demanding the Trump administration brief lawmakers on the disruptions. "It's unclear if it's all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Tuesday. The Federal Aviation Administration announced Tuesday it had paused the installation of routers linked to Friday's nationwide ground stop, which disrupted air travel across the country. The agency is still investigating what caused the ground stop. A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase also caused online banking delays, while a Microsoft outage disrupted email services. title: Rubio says 'zero' information that US outages are linked or caused by a malign actor
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's 'zero' information that a series of outages and technical failures across the U.S. are related to each other or to a malign actor. Rubio looked to calm Americans as he was traveling with President Donald Trump as they prepared to leave Manila for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. "We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said. President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications. Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected. Each outage has been blamed on internal technical problems, with the companies and government agencies involved denying that they were the result of cyberattacks or rogue artificial intelligence systems. Trump was nonchalant after arriving in Asia on Tuesday, declaring that "things like that happen," a response that did little to calm the country. Karoline Leavitt, Trump's former press secretary, offered advice for her old colleagues in the administration. "What I would say to the White House is transparency is key," Leavitt said on Fox News. She said the president or someone else at the White House should explain what they know after Trump returns from Asia "to really calm the temperature." She later praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network. "Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber attack incident," Clayton said in a clip that Leavitt shared on X. He said the U.S. government believes the incidents are caused by organizations making security upgrades that are taking longer than planned and encountering unexpected hiccups.
